entries.name: BitBox02 (BitBox02 and BitBox02 Nova, Multi and Bitcoin-only editions)
entries.purpose: Swiss open-source hardware wallets from Shift Crypto with a dual-chip design (open firmware on a microcontroller plus a secure chip). They sign Bitcoin transactions after on-device confirmation and support multisig, miniscript wallet policies (including Taproot) and sending to silent-payment addresses.

platforms.windowsDistribution: No vendor driver (USB HID). The BitBoxApp (bitboxapp) performs firmware upgrades, including mandatory intermediate versions (9.17.1, 9.26.2). The device must be paired with a host once (Noise pairing code confirmed on the device); HWI driven by another program cannot show the pairing code and tells the user to pair in the BitBoxApp first and then close it.

dependencies.notes: Firmware upgrades, initial setup and first host pairing.
Host software for xpub export, policy/multisig registration and PSBT signing.

entries.security: Dual-chip design: secure chip ATECC608B on the BitBox02, Infineon Optiga Trust M V3 (EAL6+, NDA-free) on the Nova, which also enforces the 10-attempt password limit in hardware. Reproducible firmware builds with community signatures; the firmware hash shown at start-up is published per edition (9.27.1: Bitcoin-only 2522156c…bc73, Multi 38ddfd37…5648, Nova Bitcoin-only f48bb49f…acb4, Nova Multi d65b34fe…88fc). Security fixes: 9.15.0 fixed a fee attack reported by Saleem Rashid; 9.26.3 and 9.26.5 contain 'general security improvements'. Anti-klepto is required by BitBoxApp 4.52.0 for signing. BTCortex must only display, never relay, the pairing code, and must not attempt firmware flashing.

entries.name: Bitcoin Core
entries.purpose: Reference full-node implementation of the Bitcoin protocol: downloads, validates and relays blocks and transactions, and exposes JSON-RPC, REST and ZMQ interfaces, an optional descriptor wallet and the bitcoin-qt graphical interface.

maintenance.evidence: Latest stable release 31.1 announced 2026-07-08 (files in /bin/bitcoin-core-31.1/ dated 2026-07-07). Maintained lines per the lifecycle page: 31.x, 30.x (30.3, 2026-07-08) and 29.x (29.4, announced 2026-07-13, GitHub release 2026-07-10) until 32.0 ships. 32.0rc1 tagged 2026-09-14 and 32.0rc4 on 2026-10-12 (target was 2026-10-10). Latest master commit 2026-10-20. Repository not archived.

platforms.windowsVersions: Windows 10 version 1903 or later for 31.x and 32.0 (29.x and 30.x release notes say Windows 10 or later)
platforms.windowsDistribution: Authenticode-signed NSIS installer (bitcoin-31.1-win64-setup.exe, 39 221 288 bytes) and signed portable ZIP (bitcoin-31.1-win64.zip, 54 894 985 bytes) from https://bitcoincore.org/bin/bitcoin-core-31.1/; unsigned variants (-win64-setup-unsigned.exe, -win64-unsigned.zip), a debug-symbols ZIP, a codesigning tarball and a torrent are also published. No Windows ARM64 build (Guix builds only x86_64-w64-mingw32).

dependencies.notes: SOCKS5 proxy (-proxy or -onion, typically 127.0.0.1:9050; Tor Browser uses 9150) for onion peers, and the control port (-torcontrol, default 127.0.0.1:9051) for automatic ephemeral onion services (-listenonion=1 by default when listening). Version 3 onion services only.
I2P via the SAM v3 bridge (-i2psam=<ip:port>; -i2pacceptincoming default 1). The 32.0 draft notes that legacy ElGamal I2P sessions will be removed on or before v34.
CJDNS reachability flag (-cjdnsreachable). The 32.0 release-notes draft says the project is considering dropping CJDNS support.
External signer (-signer=<cmd>, enumeratesigners, walletdisplayaddress) for hardware wallets; support on Windows was re-enabled in 30.0.
Only for the manual verification procedure on bitcoincore.org; BTCortex should verify signatures natively instead of requiring GnuPG.

Same default data directory, default install directory (C:\Program Files\Bitcoin), P2P and RPC ports, bitcoin: URI handler and bitcoin-qt registry key. Knots 29.4.1.knots20260508 and later follow an incompatible chain; never let the two share a data directory or run with the same ports.

entries.security: RPC is full control of the node and any loaded wallet (spending, chain manipulation, file writes on the host); keep it on loopback, prefer the cookie (protected by the data directory's NTFS ACL; -rpccookieperms maps only to POSIX-style bits) or rpcauth, never pass passwords on the command line, and use rpcwhitelist for scoped credentials. REST and ZMQ are unauthenticated. *notify and -signer options execute shell commands. Since 30.0 -natpmp=1 asks the router to forward the P2P port, which changes privacy exposure. Verify downloads with SHA256SUMS signed by multiple builder keys from bitcoin-core/guix.sigs; Windows executables are Authenticode-signed by 'Bitcoin Core Code Signing LLC' (DigiCert). Version warnings: <25.0 has High-severity remote crashes (CVE-2024-35202, CVE-2019-25220 <24.0.1); <29.0 is affected by CVE-2024-52911 (High, use-after-free in script validation); 30.0 and 30.1 were withdrawn because a failed legacy-wallet migration could delete wallet files; 31.0 with -privatebroadcast could leak the sender's IP (fixed in 31.1); 28.x is end of life since 2026-04-19 and 29.x becomes end of life with 32.0, after which three Medium/High issues fixed in 30.0 are due to be disclosed.

Keeper Desktop release notes ask users to verify SHA256SUMS.txt.asc against 'the Keeper release signing key' without printing its fingerprint. entries.name: Bitcoin Knots
entries.purpose: Derivative of Bitcoin Core maintained by Luke Dashjr with additional relay-policy (spam-filter) options, retained legacy wallet features, extra RPCs and GUI additions. Since 29.4.1.knots20260508 it also enforces consensus changes that Bitcoin Core does not: the BIP110 Reduced Data Temporary Softfork rules and a BLAKE2b proof-of-work hard fork.

maintenance.evidence: Latest release 29.4.2.knots20260508 published 2026-09-21 on GitHub and bitcoinknots.org; previous releases 29.4.1.knots20260508 (2026-09-02), 29.4.knots20260508 (2026-08-07), 29.3.knots20260508 (2026-05-09), 29.3.knots20260507 (2026-05-08) and 29.3.knots20260210 (2026-02-10). Still based on the Bitcoin Core 29.x code line (default branch 29.x-knots; no 30.x or 31.x Knots branch). Repository pushed 2026-09-21; not archived.

platforms.windowsVersions: Windows 10 or later (per the 29.4.x release notes)
platforms.windowsDistribution: NSIS installer bitcoin-29.4.2.knots20260508-win64-setup-pgpverifiable.exe and portable ZIP bitcoin-29.4.2.knots20260508-win64-pgpverifiable.zip from https://bitcoinknots.org/files/29.x/29.4.2.knots20260508/ (also attached to the GitHub release). 'pgpverifiable' builds are not Authenticode-signed; integrity relies on the OpenPGP-signed SHA256SUMS.

dependencies.notes: Same Tor integration as Bitcoin Core, plus -torexecute to spawn a tor process if none is running.
I2P via SAM (-i2psam).
-cjdnsreachable as in Bitcoin Core 29.x.
External signer support (-signer) as in Bitcoin Core 29.x.

Knots' release notes direct miners on its chain to run their own DATUM Gateway, but DATUM Gateway's README (read on 2026-10-23) says Knots versions after 29.3.knots20260507 are no longer compatible with it and would earn no mining rewards; not needed for non-mining nodes.

Shares Bitcoin Core's default data directory (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Bitcoin or legacy %APPDATA%\Bitcoin), default install directory (C:\Program Files\Bitcoin), ports, bitcoin: URI handler and QSettings key, yet follows an incompatible chain since 29.4.1.knots20260508. Never share a data directory or install directory between them.

entries.security: Windows binaries are not Authenticode-signed ('pgpverifiable'), so integrity rests on SHA256SUMS signed by builder keys from bitcoinknots/guix.sigs (3 to 7 signatures on recent releases, always including Luke Dashjr's key 1A3E761F19D2CC7785C5502EA291A2C45D0C504A). Consensus divergence from Bitcoin Core creates replay and chain-confusion risk: Knots wallets sign with a new 'hardfork' signature hash by default (-walletoldsigs=1 gives up replay protection), coins created before the split exist on both chains, and wallets or services connected to a Knots node see Knots' chain. Builds stop accepting new blocks after a built-in software-expiry date (about 2028-11-06 for 29.4.2) unless softwareexpiry=0 is set. Inherits Bitcoin Core 29.x code, so Core security fixes arrive only when Knots backports them; legacy BDB wallets remain loadable.

maintenance.evidence: 2.1.3 published 2026-08-05 (2.1.2 2026-08-04, 2.1.1 2026-07-20, 2.1.0 2026-07-19). Latest main commit 2026-10-20 (merge of PR #851). pyproject.toml on main already declares 2.2.0. Repository not archived.

platforms.windowsDistribution: Bitcoin-Safe-2.1.3-setup.exe (NSIS: RequestExecutionLevel admin, default folder $PROGRAMFILES64\<product>, Add/Remove Programs entry and a bitcoin: URI handler under HKCU, desktop and Start Menu shortcuts including a 'Testnet' shortcut; the uninstaller removes only the program folder) and Bitcoin-Safe-2.1.3-portable.exe (single executable, no installer). Each has a detached OpenPGP .asc; SHA-256 values are shown on the release page. Windows binaries are Authenticode-signed through SignPath with a certificate issued by the SignPath Foundation and are reproducible (built under Wine in Docker).

dependencies.notes: As a compact-filter peer (blockfilterindex=1, peerblockfilters=1, P2P listening on loopback) or through the RPC backend type.
Electrum backend alternative to compact block filters; requires an unpruned node.
Pulled in through bitcoin-usb (hwi >= 3.2.0); no separate HWI installation is needed.

Not bundled; a SOCKS proxy can be set per network (proxy_url); a Tor onion URL is offered for the mempool.space fee data.

entries.security: Mainnet enforces hardware-only seeds, which fits BTCortex's rule of never handling mnemonics. Releases are signed with the OpenPGP key 2759 AA71 4856 8ECC B03B 7630 1D82 124B 440F 612D (published on keys.openpgp.org, which shows no identity for it); Windows binaries are Authenticode-signed through the SignPath Foundation; builds are reproducible (Windows hashes match after stripping the Authenticode signature with osslsigncode). The app verifies update signatures itself. Privacy: the code-signing policy says the default blockchain data comes from Blockstream's Electrum/Esplora servers, while the README and network configuration make compact block filters the default where available; fee data comes from mempool.space; Sync & Chat exposes encrypted traffic metadata to Nostr relays. Address-poisoning detection warns about look-alike addresses. The uninstaller does not delete user data.

entries.purpose: Rust proxy in front of bitcoind that gives each client its own credentials with an allow-list of RPC methods (and an optional forced wallet), and performs on-demand block fetching from peers so that applications see a pruned node as unpruned.

maintenance.evidence: Last release v0.4.0 on 2024-07-13; master Cargo.toml is at 0.4.1 with the latest commit 2026-08-18 ('Bump version'), not yet released.

entries.security: Finer-grained permissions than Bitcoin Core's rpcwhitelist per application; configuration files hold passwords (permissions 600 per upstream). Does not help tools that need txindex (Fulcrum, ElectrumX, mempool) or that read REST or block files directly (electrs 0.12, Esplora electrs).

entries.name: Caddy
entries.purpose: Web server and HTTPS reverse proxy with automatic certificates and an internal local certificate authority, suitable for local or LAN TLS termination in front of BTCortex-managed web interfaces.

platforms.windowsDistribution: caddy_2.11.7_windows_amd64.zip and caddy_2.11.7_windows_arm64.zip (single caddy.exe) with SBOMs; caddy_2.11.7_checksums.txt holds SHA-512 sums and is signed with Sigstore keyless signing (.sig and .pem; the certificate identity is the release workflow https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v2.11.7). Each archive also has its own .sig/.pem.

entries.security: The first use of the internal CA tries to install the 'Caddy Local Authority' root into the system trust store and prompts for permission; that root key can sign certificates trusted by the machine, so BTCortex should set skip_install_trust and distribute trust deliberately. The unauthenticated admin API on localhost:2019 lets any local process change the configuration; disable it or restrict it. Windows services must be created with sc.exe or WinSW (administrator) and cannot be reloaded through the service manager.

entries.name: Caravan
entries.purpose: Stateless, browser-based multisig coordinator (the React single-page 'Caravan Coordinator'), originally Unchained's and now developed in the caravan-bitcoin monorepo. It derives multisig addresses from xpubs, builds and broadcasts transactions and collects signatures from hardware wallets, files or BC-UR 2 QR signers, using public block-explorer APIs or a private Bitcoin Core node.

maintenance.evidence: caravan-coordinator@1.19.2 released 2026-07-20 (1.19.0 on 2026-03-02 added BC-UR 2); @caravan/wallets@0.11.0 2026-08-22; @caravan/psbt@2.1.1 and @caravan/bitcoin@0.4.6 2026-09-17. Latest commits 2026-10-15 (signature audit refactor, PR #517 from an Unchained contributor). Docker Hub caravanbitcoin/coordinator:1.19.2 pushed 2026-07-20.

platforms.windowsVersions: Not stated upstream; any Windows version that runs a current Chromium-based browser (direct device access relies on browser USB APIs)
platforms.windowsDistribution: No Windows package. Options: the hosted site (caravanmultisig.com; also linked: caravan-bitcoin.github.io/caravan and caravan-coordinator.vercel.app), the official Docker image caravanbitcoin/coordinator (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64; container port 80), or a static build from source with Node.js >= 24 and npm >= 11.10 (npm run build:coordinator).

dependencies.notes: A private Bitcoin Core node behind a CORS proxy, or a public Esplora/mempool API (unchained.mempool.space by default).
Keystores in @caravan/wallets; QR signers through BC-UR 2.

entries.security: Caravan holds no keys; signatures are produced on devices or by external signers after explicit user action. Loading the coordinator from a hosted origin means trusting remote JavaScript that sees xpubs and, in private mode, the node's RPC credentials; a locally served copy is preferable. The CORS proxy must allow only the Caravan origin and RPC must stay on loopback; the README stresses that CORS headers 'are essential to protecting the security of your coins'. Public mode reveals every wallet address to the API operator (Unchained's mempool.space instance or Blockstream). Supply-chain hardening: a 7-day npm min-release-age in .npmrc.

entries.name: chantools
entries.purpose: Rescue tool for funds locked in LND channels when LND itself cannot run properly, for example zombie channels or channels force-closed by the peer; some commands also support Core Lightning.

platforms.windowsDistribution: ZIP archive chantools-windows-amd64-v0.14.3.zip, with manifest-v0.14.3.txt and its signature

entries.security: Many commands need the wallet seed; the README says it never leaves the computer and that typing it in the terminal is the safest way. Some commands query public block explorers, which costs privacy. forceclose publishes an old channel state and is only for peers that are gone for good. The README warns that it was built for particular rescue operations and should be reviewed before serious use.

entries.name: cjdns
entries.purpose: Encrypted IPv6 mesh network (addresses in fc00::/8 derived from public keys, DHT routing). Bitcoin Core can use it as an additional network with -cjdnsreachable. It encrypts end to end but does not hide sender and recipient from intermediate routers.

maintenance.evidence: Tags cjdns-v22.1 to cjdns-v22.3; latest master commit 2025-12-10 ('Release 22.3 ThirtyTwo - Bug fix release which fixes 32bit'). The Windows installation document was last changed on 2017-01-18.

platforms.windowsDistribution: No Windows binaries. doc/install/windows.md describes cross-compiling cjdroute.exe from Linux with mingw (SYSTEM=win32), installing the OpenVPN TAP-Windows driver and running cjdroute from an elevated command prompt; the README's installation instructions cover only Linux and macOS (pre-built binaries via cjdns.sh for Linux amd64).

entries.security: Requires a kernel network driver and administrator rights on Windows. Bitcoin Core's documentation: 'CJDNS is fast but does not hide the sender and the recipient from intermediate routers', so it must not be presented as anonymity.

entries.name: ckpool
entries.purpose: Low-overhead, massively scalable mining pool server in C for Linux, which also works as a proxy, passthrough, node, redirector or solo pool (BTCSOLO mode).

maintenance.evidence: The Bitbucket repository was updated on 2026-10-14; it publishes no releases.

entries.security: Its README asks operators to keep the default 0.5% development contribution on blocks found in pool mode.

entries.name: cloudflared (Cloudflare Tunnel)
entries.purpose: Daemon that makes outbound-only connections to Cloudflare's network so that local services can be published or reached through Cloudflare without opening inbound ports (a hosted reverse tunnel).

platforms.windowsDistribution: cloudflared-windows-amd64.exe/.msi and cloudflared-windows-386.exe/.msi on GitHub Releases.

entries.security: All tunnelled traffic passes through a third party that the user must trust; it is not anonymity and creates an account-linked public endpoint. BTCortex must never publish node RPC, Electrum or Lightning management interfaces this way. Tor onion services provide inbound reachability without a third-party account.

entries.name: COLDCARD
entries.purpose: Bitcoin-only signing devices from Coinkite (COLDCARD Mk4, Mk5 and Q) built for air-gapped PSBT signing over microSD, NFC and (Q only) QR/BBQr, with optional USB, multisig with up to 15 co-signers, descriptor export and, on the separate EDGE firmware track, miniscript and Taproot script policies.

maintenance.evidence: Standard firmware 5.6.3 (Mk4/Mk5) and 1.5.3Q (Q) dated 2026-09-30 in releases/ChangeLog.md; releases/signatures.txt clear-signed 2026-09-30T20:27Z. Earlier: 5.6.2/1.5.2Q 2026-09-03, 5.6.1/1.5.1Q 2026-08-20, 5.5.1/1.4.1Q 2026-07-01, 5.4.5/1.3.5Q 2025-11-03. EDGE builds 6.6.1X/6.6.1QX dated 2026-08-31. Latest master commit 2026-10-09 ('Fix Shamir split share-count prompt on Mk4 and Mk5'). GitHub Releases are not used: binaries are on coldcard.com/downloads and hashes in releases/signatures.txt. Mk3/Mk2 are on their final release 4.2.0 and Mk1 on 3.0.6. ckcc-protocol 1.6.0 was published to PyPI on 2026-09-08.

platforms.windowsDistribution: Nothing has to be installed for air-gapped use: a microSD card reader, or a webcam or phone for the Q's QR and NFC. USB data uses the HID-based COLDCARD protocol (hidapi in ckcc-protocol and HWI); Virtual Disk mode emulates a 4 MB USB disk that the Q documentation lists as working on Windows. Coinkite documents download verification on Windows with Gpg4win/Kleopatra and certutil -hashfile <file> SHA256.

dependencies.notes: A coordinator or watch-only wallet builds PSBTs, tracks the wallet and broadcasts; COLDCARD only signs.
USB discovery, xpub and descriptor retrieval, address display and signing with on-device approval. Not needed for microSD, NFC or QR workflows.

entries.security: July 2026 seed-generation incident (advisory published 2026-07-30, updated 2026-08-01): a firmware bug weakened device-generated entropy and attackers regenerated affected private keys offline and stole funds. Affected: Mk2/Mk3 firmware 4.0.1 to 4.1.9 (most severe); seeds generated on Mk4/Mk5 before 5.6.0, on Q before 1.5.0Q and on EDGE before 6.6.0X/6.6.0QX (about 72 instead of 128 bits). Updating does not repair an existing seed: such wallets must be migrated to a new seed unless at least 50 private, fair dice rolls were added. TAPSIGNER, OPENDIME and SATSCARD are stated to be unaffected. BTCortex cannot tell from an xpub which firmware generated a seed, so it must show the advisory and the minimum fixed release per track (5.6.0, 1.5.0Q, 4.2.0, 6.6.0X/6.6.0QX; recommended 5.6.3/1.5.3Q) whenever a COLDCARD is detected or chosen, and never offer to 'check' a seed. Firmware authenticity: the device only runs factory-signed firmware (red CAUTION LED until an upgrade is blessed, green GENUINE LED afterwards); downloads are verified with releases/signatures.txt, a SHA-256 list clear-signed by OpenPGP key 4589779ADFC14F3327534EA8A3A31BAD5A2A5B10 (Peter D. Gray, DocHex on Keybase; issuer confirmed from the 2026-09-30 signature). Recent hardening: SIGHASH_SINGLE blocked by default, re-verification of the staged PSBT before signing, rejection of duplicate inputs and negative amounts, authenticated USB encryption v3, removal of the unused USB serial interface, warnings before externally signed firmware or downgrades. BTCortex must never send passphrases or seed material, never enable HSM mode and never sign without the user approving on the device.

entries.name: electrs (Electrum Rust Server)
entries.purpose: Efficient Electrum-protocol server in Rust for personal and small-scale use. It keeps a compact index (about 7 % of the block data) and fetches transactions from the local Bitcoin Core node on demand. Since 0.12.0 it is built on the bindex library and reads blocks through Bitcoin Core's REST interface.

maintenance.evidence: v0.12.0 published 2026-09-13 (0.11.1 on 2026-02-22, 0.11.0 on 2025-11-17, 0.10.10 on 2025-07-19). Latest master commit 2026-10-17. Repository not archived. Cargo.toml version 0.12.0 depends on bindex 0.1.2 (bindex-rs v0.1.3 tagged 2026-09-28).

platforms.windowsDistribution: No official binaries for any platform ('There are currently no official/stable binary packages'). Source build only (Rust 1.85 or later, libclang for rust-rocksdb). Windows-specific code exists: the ctrlc crate replaces signal-hook on Windows since 0.10.8 (PR #1123, December 2024, which also added a Windows CI build without the Prometheus metrics feature). The current CI workflow only builds on ubuntu-latest.

dependencies.notes: Core 31.0 or later, rest=1, server=1, prune=0. The REST interface is unauthenticated and shares the RPC listener.
Onion service (HiddenServicePort 50001 127.0.0.1:50001) gives remote wallets an encrypted, authenticated-by-address path without a TLS proxy.
TLS termination for SSL clients (upstream documents an nginx stream block on port 50002).
Same default client port 50001 and the same role.

entries.security: Optimised for personal or family use. SECURITY.md: 'Denial-of-Service attacks are excluded from the threat model - DO NOT share your electrs instance with untrusted users!'. No TLS of its own. 0.12.0 requires Bitcoin Core's REST interface, which is unauthenticated and served wherever the RPC listener is bound, so RPC/REST must stay on loopback (or a host-only WSL network) and never be exposed to the LAN. Upstream recommends cookie authentication. auto_reindex (default true) silently rebuilds an inconsistent or old-format database, which takes hours. Default daemon_dir is ~/.bitcoin even on Windows, so a wrong guess silently points at the wrong node; always pass daemon_dir and cookie_file. No GitHub security advisories published as of 2026-10-21.

entries.name: Electrum
entries.purpose: Long-established lightweight (SPV) Bitcoin wallet with Lightning support. It verifies headers and merkle proofs itself but needs an Electrum-protocol server for wallet history; supports hardware wallets through vendor plugins, multisig, watch-only wallets, PSBT files and QR codes, and a JSON-RPC daemon.

maintenance.evidence: Release 4.8.2 on 2026-09-11 (security update), 4.8.1 on 2026-08-10, 4.8.0 on 2026-07-08, 4.7.2 on 2026-04-01, 4.7.1 on 2026-02-26, 4.7.0 on 2026-01-22; every release since 4.7.0 is labelled a security update. Latest master commit 2026-10-20 (11e3aa9d20). Repository not archived. A 4.9 milestone with planned compatibility breaks is open (issue #10989).

platforms.windowsVersions: Windows 10 version 1809 or later (older versions may need KB2999226)
platforms.windowsDistribution: Three Windows x86_64 PyInstaller builds per release from download.electrum.org/<version>/: electrum-<v>-setup.exe (NSIS installer; requires administrator rights and quits with error 740 otherwise; installs to %ProgramFiles%\Electrum, wipes the install folder on upgrade, writes HKCU uninstall and URI-handler keys for bitcoin:, lightning:, lnurlp: and lnurlw:), electrum-<v>.exe (standalone single executable using %APPDATA%\Electrum) and electrum-<v>-portable.exe (single executable that keeps its data in an electrum_data folder in the working directory). All are Authenticode-signed and each has a detached .asc file with several developer signatures. Reproducible builds.

dependencies.notes: A self-hosted Electrum server for privacy (oneserver=true, server 127.0.0.1:50002:s, serverfingerprint). Without one, Electrum uses public servers.
SOCKS5 proxy (proxy socks5:127.0.0.1:9050, enable_proxy true) for public or onion servers; Electrum does not ship Tor.
USB signers through Electrum's own plugins (vendor libraries such as trezorlib 0.20+, ledger_bitcoin 0.4.1+, bitbox02 7.0.0).

entries.security: Electrum holds private keys for standard and multisig software wallets; BTCortex must never create seed-based wallets in it, never read wallet files and never handle seeds. Every release since 4.7.0 is a security update; 4.7.2 fixed a medium-severity external-plugin authorisation bypass leading to local code execution (GHSA-vw94-r84p-66qf) and 4.8.0 a low-severity SPV issue (CVE-2012-2459 duplicate-leaf merkle trees), so outdated installations (such as 4.7.2 on the test machine) must be flagged. 4.7.1 warned that malicious translations had injected Bitcoin addresses into UI strings, causing a user to lose funds. Release verification: each binary has a detached .asc containing several signatures; for 4.8.2 (signed 2026-09-12) these are ThomasV 6694 D8DE 7BE8 EE56 31BE D950 2BD5 824B 7F94 70E6, SomberNight's release key 0EED CFD5 CAFB 4590 6734 9B23 CA9E EEC4 3DF9 11DC, Emzy (signing subkey 637D B1E2 3370 F84A FF88 CCE0 3152 347D 07DA 627C of primary 9EDA FF80 E080 6596 04F4 A76B 2EBB 056F D847 F8A7; that subkey expired on 2026-10-12 in the copy shipped with 4.8.2), felixb_f321x AA0B C682 4B39 7BBA 9977 6E15 7ED8 D82B 3719 2688 (NIST P-256) and svanstaa 33C1 03B4 B279 4170 546C CF7B CFB2 C83C 66CD 792A. Require at least ThomasV's or SomberNight's release-key signature; do not require Emzy's signature, which strict verifiers may reject after the expiry. Binaries are also Authenticode-signed. Using public servers reveals addresses; oneserver should only be used with a fully trusted (own) server, and serverfingerprint pins it. Electrum binaries are often flagged by antivirus heuristics (download page).

entries.name: Electrum Personal Server (EPS)
entries.purpose: Lightweight single-user Electrum server that imports the user's master public keys and addresses as watch-only into a Bitcoin Core wallet instead of indexing the whole chain; it worked with pruned nodes, blocksonly and txindex=0.

maintenance.evidence: Last release 0.2.4 on 2022-06-16 and last commit the same day. Repository not archived. Issue #309 (opened 2025-05-18) asks whether Bitcoin Core 30's removal of legacy wallets ends EPS; it has no maintainer reply. PR #313 (2025-12-07) adding descriptor-wallet support is open, unreviewed and unmerged.

platforms.windowsDistribution: electrum-personal-server-windows-release-v0.2.4.zip with an OpenPGP signature (.asc) on the GitHub release; the README tells Windows users to drag config.ini onto the packaged executable.

dependencies.notes: Only versions before 30.0 (legacy wallet and importmulti); wallet enabled, server=1.

entries.security: Ships a default TLS certificate whose private key is public, so connections can be decrypted unless the user generates their own. Single client at a time. The watch-only wallet reveals the user's addresses to anyone with RPC access to the node. Unmaintained since 2022. Its legacy-wallet design cannot work with supported Bitcoin Core versions.

entries.name: ElectrumX
entries.purpose: Python (asyncio) Electrum-protocol server maintained by the Electrum developers (the spesmilo fork of Neil Booth's original). Widely used for public Electrum servers, multi-coin, and the first server to implement Electrum protocol 1.7.

maintenance.evidence: 2.0.0 released 2026-07-03 (changelog date; GitHub release entry and PyPI package e-x 2.0.0 uploaded the same day); 1.20.0 on 2026-06-03, 1.19.0 on 2025-11-11, 1.18.0 on 2025-06-14, 1.17.0 on 2025-04-16. Latest master commit 2026-07-03. The original kyuupichan/electrumx last released 1.20.2 on 2021-10-28 and is not the maintained Bitcoin line.

dependencies.notes: Core 31.0 or later, txindex=1, txospenderindex=1, unpruned; rpcauth credentials.
Onion service for clients; TOR_PROXY_HOST/PORT (autodetects 9050, 9150, 1080) for onion peers; FORCE_PROXY to route peer discovery through Tor.
Same conventional ports 50001/50002 and the same role.

entries.security: Public-server features (peer discovery and self-announcement) are enabled by default and leak the host's existence and IP unless disabled. LocalRPC is unauthenticated. 1.19.0 fixed a denial-of-service vector (new sessions refused after MAX_SESSIONS on Python 3.12+); 1.16.0 fixed a remote crash when peer discovery was enabled. The DAEMON_URL embeds the RPC password in an environment variable, so keep the process environment private and use a dedicated, whitelisted rpcauth user. No GitHub security advisories published as of 2026-10-21.

Bundled Tor service and ONION_URL for the Onion-Location header.

entries.name: Frostsnap
entries.purpose: Distributed signing devices that use FROST threshold Schnorr signatures (Taproot) so that, for example, any two of three daisy-chained devices can sign for a wallet that looks single-sig on chain; coordinated by the Frostsnap app on Android, Windows, macOS and Linux.

maintenance.evidence: v0.4.0 published 2026-08-25 (security fixes), v0.3.0 August 2026, v0.2.x 2026; latest master commit 2026-10-20. Devices orderable at 150,000 sats each (frostsnap.com, 2026-10-21).

platforms.windowsDistribution: The coordinator app has a Windows x64 build: Frostsnap-v0.4.0.zip, the zipped Flutter release folder (portable, no installer; CI builds it on windows-latest). Each asset has a detached .asc signature and CHECKSUMS/CHECKSUMS.asc are provided, signed by the key 'Frostsnap <security@frostsnap.com>' (primary F19CCCCD876B6E57FB712206A9D5981F42B0EA50, signing subkey A0D99F559A2E20CFE6D18ABDFE2521845E568DAE). Devices connect over USB-C.

dependencies.notes: A self-hosted Electrum server could back the app; configuring it was not verified.

entries.security: Threshold design removes the single point of failure of one device; keys are generated collaboratively with entropy from the phone or laptop. Devices have no PIN or secure element. v0.4.0 fixed a malicious-app attack that could get a device to sign an output hidden from its confirmation screen, and change addresses that could fall outside the recovery scan range; it also blocks firmware downgrades and publishes a deterministic firmware digest. FROST signing is not PSBT multisig: standard coordinators cannot co-sign, and recovery depends on Frostsnap's backup format. Young 0.x project without a published third-party audit.

entries.name: Fulcrum
entries.purpose: Fast, multi-threaded C++20 Electrum-protocol (SPV) server for Bitcoin, Bitcoin Cash and Litecoin. It indexes the whole chain from a txindex-enabled full node and serves script-hash history, balances, UTXOs, headers and merkle proofs to Electrum-protocol wallets such as Sparrow and Electrum.

maintenance.evidence: Release 2.1.4 published 2026-10-18 (2.1.3 on 2026-10-02, 2.1.2 on 2026-08-20, 2.1.1 on 2026-05-07, 2.1.0 on 2025-11-19). Latest master commit 2026-10-18 ('Refreshed servers*.json for BCH and BTC'). Repository not archived. Docker Hub image cculianu/fulcrum:v2.1.4 pushed 2026-10-18.

platforms.windowsVersions: Windows 10 or later, 64-bit (release notes: it should 'just work' on any Windows 10 or above 64-bit system)
platforms.windowsDistribution: Portable ZIP only: Fulcrum-2.1.4-win64.zip (17 168 090 bytes) with a statically linked Fulcrum.exe (jemalloc, libzmq, libminiupnpc, Qt 6.10, OpenSSL 3.3.0, gcc 15.2.0) and FulcrumAdmin.exe (the Python admin script packed as a PyInstaller one-file executable). No installer. Checksums in Fulcrum-2.1.4-shasums.txt, signed in Fulcrum-2.1.4-shasums.txt.asc. MSVC builds are unsupported; MinGW is used.

dependencies.notes: Unpruned node with txindex=1 and RPC. zmqpubhashblock recommended. Enabling txindex on an existing node starts a background index build; getindexinfo reports synced=false until it finishes. Keep rpcthreads above bitcoind_clients (default 3) plus the other RPC clients.

Onion service for remote wallets (HiddenServicePort to 127.0.0.1:50001/50002) and tor_proxy (default 127.0.0.1:9050) for discovering .onion peers. tor_hostname and tor_*_port only matter when announcing to the public server network.
All three use the conventional ports 50001/50002 and the same client-facing role. Run only one Electrum server per port set and per wallet profile.

entries.security: The server learns every address its clients query, so only a self-hosted server preserves wallet privacy. Admin RPC and /stats are unauthenticated and must stay on loopback. The 0.0.0.0 default TCP bind would expose the server to the LAN unless BTCortex writes loopback binds. Disable peering and announce on private servers to avoid outbound connections and advertising the host. TLS: RSA keys are fully supported, EC/DH/DSA keys are 'experimental'. Certificates can be replaced without a restart (SSLCertMonitor). Release verification: SHA-256 checksums in Fulcrum-<version>-shasums.txt, signed by Calin Culianu's DSA-2048 OpenPGP key D465 135F 97D0 047E 18E9 9DC3 2181 0A54 2031 C02C (signature verified for 2.1.4 on 2026-10-21; key published in Electron-Cash/keys-n-hashes). Antivirus heuristics have flagged FulcrumAdmin.exe (PyInstaller one-file) as a false positive (issue #203), so BTCortex should talk to the admin port directly rather than launch FulcrumAdmin.exe. Prefer cookie authentication to bitcoind. No GitHub security advisories published as of 2026-10-21. Use 2.1.1 or later on Windows: it fixes spammy Win32 API handle exhaustion messages with BTC (issue #324).

entries.name: HWI (Hardware Wallet Interface)
entries.purpose: Python library (hwilib) and command-line tool from the Bitcoin Core organisation that gives one JSON interface to USB hardware wallets: enumerate devices, export xpubs and output descriptors, display addresses on the device and sign PSBTs. It is the reference external signer for Bitcoin Core's -signer option.

maintenance.evidence: Release 3.2.0 on 2026-02-10 (3.1.0 on 2024-09-17, 3.0.0 on 2024-04-06). Latest master commit 2026-08-25 ('Optionally pass BIP388 policy to signtx', unreleased). Pinned issue #850 'Future of this repo' (achow101, 2026-08-18): no new features or device support except MuSig2, the next release 'will likely be the final release of HWI', then minimal maintenance and archiving once a replacement is ready; BHWI is named as a promising successor. Repository not archived.

platforms.windowsDistribution: Portable ZIP hwi-3.2.0-windows-x86_64.zip (60 113 236 bytes) containing hwi.exe (command line) and hwi-qt.exe (GUI), both PyInstaller builds; no installer. SHA-256 values for the ZIP and for both executables inside it are in SHA256SUMS.txt.asc (clear-signed). Also a Python wheel and source package (Python >=3.9,<3.13).

dependencies.notes: Devices driven by HWI 3.2.0 (see interfaces for model limits).
Watch-only descriptor import, PSBT funding (walletcreatefundedpsbt), finalisation and broadcast; or Core's own -signer integration.
Applications that hold the same USB interface or COM port. Close them before an HWI session (BitBox02 pairing is the exception: it must be done in the BitBoxApp first, which must then be closed).

entries.security: HWI never sees seeds; it relays requests that the device must approve on its own screen. BTCortex must still treat it as a powerful tool: setup, restore, wipe, backup and passphrase options touch seed management and must never be exposed; signtx must only follow an explicit user action, with the PSBT reviewed in BTCortex and on the device; displayaddress should be offered before a receive address is used. Release verification: SHA256SUMS.txt.asc is clear-signed by Ava Chow (achow101), RSA-4096 key 1528 1230 0785 C964 44D3 334D 1756 5732 E08E 5E41 (created 2015-03-05, expires 2027-08-21; the 3.2.0 signature from 2026-02-10 verified on 2026-10-21 with the key from bitcoin-core/guix.sigs builder-keys); 3.2.0 hashes: ZIP 2f1a5574647e3ce11b1a05feab2fcbbf17061937c970d321d7f4c28a7b6eca23, hwi.exe e068d91b664597425a8ead02d7b86a02ad6c4b72746c42961f58a58b08f9fd79, hwi-qt.exe 10300209bb1fb27a9c9eb1804ae4414de534c2028d55a57d8618835ba6822a9f. Verify the inner hwi.exe hash after extraction too. Device-specific limits: Trezor removed non-wallet-input signing (One firmware 1.10.6+, Model T/Safe 2.4.4+); Trezor has no descriptor registration; the published support matrix is partly outdated (it marks BitBox02 Taproot unsupported although the driver handles it). Do not reuse third-party copies of hwi.exe (for example the fork bundled by Nunchuk) for BTCortex's own integration. HWI's winding-down (issue #850) means new devices and firmware changes will not be followed; BTCortex must design its signer adapter so that HWI can be replaced (BHWI, vendor libraries, or delegation to Sparrow).

entries.name: I2P (Java I2P router)
entries.purpose: The reference Java implementation of the I2P anonymity network, with a router console, I2PTunnel, I2PSnark and a SAM bridge that is off by default.

maintenance.evidence: 2.13.0 announced 2026-07-20 (post-quantum NTCP2, SSU1 removed). The GitHub mirror shows a tag 'i2p-2.14.0' on 2026-10-20 and 'i2p-2.13.0-9-rc' on 2026-10-16, but on 2026-10-21 the downloads page still listed 2.13.0 and files.i2p.net had no 2.14.0 files. geti2p.net now redirects to i2p.net.

platforms.windowsDistribution: i2pinstall_2.13.0_windows.exe (about 27 MB, requires a Java runtime) and I2P-Windows-Easy-Install-Bundle.exe (beta, bundles a Java runtime, about 171 MB). The downloads page offers OpenPGP .sig files only for the .jar, the macOS .dmg and the source tarball (key 70D2 0607 38BE F805 23AC AFF7 D75C 03B3 9B5E 14E1, idk/eyedeekay); the release post's SHA-256 list names 'i2pinstall_2.13.0-0_windows.exe', which does not match the published file name, and lists no Easy-Install bundle.

entries.security: Weaker download verification for Windows than for i2pd: no signature for the Windows installers on the downloads page and a checksum list whose Windows file name does not match. The SAM bridge is off by default, so enabling it changes the router's configuration.

entries.name: i2pd (I2P daemon)
entries.purpose: Lightweight C++ router for the I2P anonymity network. It enables the SAM bridge by default, which Bitcoin Core uses through -i2psam to make and accept I2P peer connections.

maintenance.evidence: 3.0.0 released 2026-10-20 (full SAM 3.3, I2PControl LocalDestinationInfo, keys files readable by owner only); 2.61.0 on 2026-07-20; 2.60.0 on 2026-04-25. Default branch 'openssl' pushed 2026-10-20.

platforms.windowsVersions: A separate Windows XP-compatible build is offered; the minimum for the main builds is not stated.
platforms.windowsDistribution: i2pd_<version>_win64_mingw.zip, i2pd_<version>_win32_mingw.zip, i2pd_<version>_winxp_mingw.zip and setup_i2pd_v<version>.exe on GitHub Releases. Release builds are Win32 tray applications. 2.61.0 has SHA512SUMS and SHA512SUMS.asc (issuer 9519 28BB 3170 24EF D053 D73C 66F6 C87B 98EB CFE2, R4SAS); the 3.0.0 release had no SHA512SUMS or signature on 2026-10-21.

entries.security: Unlike Tor, the receiver of an I2P connection sees the initiator's I2P address (Core's i2p.md), so transient addresses (i2pacceptincoming=0) are preferable when inbound is not needed. Disable UPnP for BTCortex-managed routers (Windows GUI builds enable it by default) and bind every local service to 127.0.0.1. Change the default I2PControl password. A non-administrator user who sees the Windows Firewall prompt for i2pd's transport listener gets block rules whatever they choose; I2P still works outbound but is reachability-limited. Verify the 2.61.0-style SHA512SUMS.asc when present; for 3.0.0 no signature was published at the time of checking.

entries.name: Blockstream Jade
entries.purpose: Open-source hardware signing devices from Blockstream (Jade Classic, Jade Plus and Jade Core) for Bitcoin and Liquid, connecting over USB serial, Bluetooth LE or air-gapped QR, with a blind-oracle PIN model, multisig registration and BIP-388 miniscript wallet policies.

maintenance.evidence: Firmware 1.0.41 dated 2026-08-22 in CHANGELOG.md ('important security updates; All users should upgrade as soon as possible'); 1.0.40 2026-04-30, 1.0.39 2026-03-06, 1.0.38 2025-11-26. Tags go up to 1.0.41; GitHub Releases are not used (firmware is served from jadefw.blockstream.com). Latest master commit 2026-10-16. Jade Core launched 2026-04-28; Blockstream's lineup post of 2026-06-02 lists Jade Classic, Jade Core and Jade Plus.

platforms.windowsDistribution: USB appears as a serial (COM) port, not HID. Blockstream's Windows troubleshooting offers two drivers when the device is not recognised: the WCH USB-serial driver and the Silicon Labs CP210x Universal Windows Driver; it does not say which model needs which. HWI recognises Silicon Labs (10c4:ea60), WCH (1a86:55d4, 1a86:7523), FTDI (0403:6001) and Espressif (303a:4001, 303a:1001) USB IDs. Only one application may hold the COM port at a time. QR mode needs a webcam on the PC; Bluetooth LE is used by the Blockstream app.

dependencies.notes: A companion or coordinator wallet builds PSBTs, relays PIN-server requests and broadcasts.
USB discovery, xpubs, descriptors, multisig/policy registration, address display and signing with on-device approval (Jade Plus support and native PSBT signing since HWI 3.2.0).
The PIN server has an onion address; routing the companion's PIN-server requests through Tor hides the user's IP address from Blockstream.

entries.security: Blind-oracle PIN model: the PIN server cannot learn the PIN or keys but is needed to unlock; it sees the IP address of whoever relays the request unless Tor is used. Official units only run Blockstream-signed firmware installed through OTA; hashes (cmphash, fwhash) are published per hardware type in index.json and the fwhash is shown on the device before installation; builds are reproducible (REPRODUCIBLE.md). 1.0.41 (2026-08-22) is a security release: stack protection, a secure-version counter that blocks downgrades, extra per-device entropy for the initial seed and better memory scrubbing. Attestation (RSA-4096) on ESP32-S3 units and 'Genuine Check' on Jade Core. Wallets are locked to MAIN or TEST networks. DIY builds are unsigned unless the builder enables secure boot. BTCortex must never use Recovery Phrase Login, SeedQR or BIP-85 features on the user's behalf.

entries.name: Keystone

maintenance.evidence: keystone3-firmware 3.1.4 published 2026-10-16 (Web3, BTC Only and Cypherpunk editions), 3.1.2 2026-10-10, 3.1.0 2026-09-17, 3.0.8 2026-09-15; 2.9.11 (2026-10-16) is an intermediate firmware for devices below 2.0.0.

entries.security: Releases publish the firmware SHA-256 and source SHA-256 for each edition; the device displays the installed firmware hash for comparison; docs/verify.md describes a Docker-based reproducible build (16 GB RAM, 32 GB recommended). No OpenPGP-signed manifests are published. Keystone recommends comparing the first receive address on the device with the coordinator and not scanning QR codes that the device did not generate. The BTC Only edition reduces the attack surface compared with Web3. BTCortex must not use the Shamir or seed features.

entries.name: Krux
entries.purpose: Open-source signing firmware for off-the-shelf Kendryte K210 devices (M5StickV, Maix Amigo and others) that signs PSBTs over QR codes or SD card and supports multisig, Taproot and wsh miniscript descriptors.

maintenance.evidence: v26.09.0 published 2026-10-03 (first release by the new maintainer jdlcdl, who took over from Odudex); 26.08.0 2026-08-04, 26.04.0 2026-04-27, 26.03.0 2026-03-26, 25.10.1 2025-10-30. entries.security: No secure element on K210 boards; mnemonics can be stored encrypted with the KEF format (AES modes including GCM). Advisories: 24.11.1 fixed AES-CBC encrypted mnemonics whose initialisation vector did not add the intended entropy; 26.09.0 fixed a 12-byte buffer overflow in GCM tag handling (assessed as non-critical, no user action needed). Releases: SHA256SUMS signed with the selfcustody ECDSA firmware key (.sig, DER, public key selfcustody.pem in the repository; the signature covers SHA256SUMS since 26.09.0) and with the maintainer's OpenPGP key (.asc; issuer 6DC76DC81B5C35D7F432712945D7F41053AF05F3 on the 26.09.0 signature); reproducible builds (firmware.bin, kboot.kfpkg, ktool) per ATTESTATION.txt. The project describes itself as research and development and requires acknowledging a disclaimer since 26.09.0. Hardware availability risk: K210 is discontinued.

entries.security: Secure element (ST33K1M5, CC EAL6+ on the Nano S Plus; Nano X listed as EAL5+); Ledger OS is closed source, the Bitcoin app is open source. Ledger Recover (opt-in, identity-based subscription service provided by Coincover) splits encrypted seed entropy into three fragments held by Coincover, Ledger and EscrowTech (two needed for recovery); its 2023 announcement was controversial because it showed that the firmware can export seed material when the user consents. BTCortex must never promote or automate it. Incidents: Ledger Connect Kit npm supply-chain attack on 2023-12-14 (malicious versions 1.1.5-1.1.7 of a web library live for about five hours; Ledger says it did not affect devices or Ledger Live) and the e-commerce/marketing database breach of 2020-06-25 (about one million email addresses, 9 500 postal details), which keeps fuelling phishing. Bitcoin app hardening: 2.4.6 rejects miniscript policies with meaningless older(n); 2.5.0 requires a persistent setting to sign non-standard sighash flags. BTCortex: verify addresses on the device, store policy HMACs per wallet, never ask for the 24 words.

entries.purpose: Desktop Bitcoin wallet focused on security, privacy and coin control. Latest master commit 2026-10-20 (b9d3bbbf64). Repository not archived; 244 open issues on 2026-10-21. Essentially a single lead developer (Craig Raw), who also signs the releases.

platforms.windowsVersions: Windows 10 and later (download page)
platforms.windowsDistribution: Two official x64 artefacts per release: Sparrow-2.5.5.msi (94.3 MB; per-user WiX MSI built by jpackage with --win-per-user-install, Start-menu group 'Sparrow', desktop shortcut, file associations for .psbt, .txn and .asc, and URI handlers for bitcoin:, lightning: and auth47:) and Sparrow-2.5.5.zip (93 MB; standalone jpackage application image with its own Java runtime, no installer). SHA-256 checksums of all artefacts are in sparrow-2.5.5-manifest.txt, signed in sparrow-2.5.5-manifest.txt.asc. No arm64 build for Windows.

dependencies.notes: Direct back end (serverType BITCOIN_CORE): Core 24.0+, server=1, wallet enabled, synchronised; pruned nodes work with the rescan limits described above. Keep the cormorant wallet loaded at every node start and never unload, modify or delete it.

Private Electrum back end (serverType ELECTRUM_SERVER), for example ssl://127.0.0.1:50002 with the server certificate in electrumServerCert. Requires an unpruned node, so not possible on the pruned test machine.

External SOCKS proxy via useProxy=true and proxyServer=127.0.0.1:9050; without a proxy, Sparrow starts its own internal Tor for .onion servers. Connecting to Bitcoin Core over Tor is documented as 'fairly slow'.
Silent-payment (BIP352) wallets need an SP-capable Electrum server; Cormorant refuses them ('Scanning silent payment wallets is not currently supported with Bitcoin Core').
USB signers through the Lark library (OneKey Classic 1S/Pro too).
Air-gapped signers via QR (UR or BBQr) or microSD files; Sparrow has import formats for each.
Screenless smartcards via a PC/SC reader; Sparrow advises small to medium amounts only.
Knots 29.4.1+ is a different chain; never pre-wire Sparrow to it without an explicit, informed user choice.

entries.security: Sparrow holds private keys only for software (hot) wallets it creates or imports; BTCortex must never create or import seed-based wallets in it and should steer users to hardware, air-gapped or watch-only keystores. Wallet databases under %APPDATA%\Sparrow\wallets are encrypted with the user's password when one is set; BTCortex must never read, copy or back them up without explicit consent. The config file is plain JSON: with cookie authentication it holds only URLs and paths, but USERPASS stores coreAuth 'user:password' in clear text, so prefer the cookie locally and a dedicated rpcauth user with an rpcwhitelist of the 22 Cormorant methods remotely. In Core mode Sparrow fully trusts the node (no merkle-proof verification); a private Electrum server learns the wallet's addresses, public servers expose them to third parties (Sparrow itself warns against public servers for significant funds). TLS certificates are pinned on first use under certs\<host>. Release verification: sparrow-<v>-manifest.txt is signed by Craig Raw's RSA-4096 key D4D0 D320 2FC0 6849 A257 B38D E946 1833 4C67 4B40 (created 2019-10-03, expires 2027-09-18; the 2.5.5 signature made 2026-09-17 with SHA-512 was verified on 2026-10-21 with the key from keybase.io/craigraw), then compare the SHA-256 of the artefact (2.5.5: ZIP da62b27effb93e83cc8fba4705248a03ec6683577c32aa6bc32801dc3b89b6e7, MSI 0256eb5c8808157f811d57fbdb9f9153101b02947c2f6788f1e7b9da5ff6111f). Pin the fingerprint, not the expiry date, and re-fetch the key when it is extended. The MSI registers bitcoin:, lightning: and auth47: URI handlers and .psbt/.txn/.asc associations, which can silently replace another wallet's handlers; the ZIP does not. Signing is always started by the user in Sparrow and confirmed on the device; BTCortex never triggers it. No GitHub security advisories were found for the repository on 2026-10-21 (not exhaustively checked).

entries.purpose: Python/Flask wallet coordinator with an Electron desktop shell that uses Bitcoin Core (or an Electrum server through its bundled Spectrum adapter) as a watch-only back end for single-signature and multisignature wallets whose keys stay on hardware wallets and air-gapped signers. Latest master commit 2026-09-03 (#2702, Specter-DIY xpub import); repository pushed 2026-10-20, not archived, 253 open issues. No maintenance-mode or discontinuation announcement was found. The 2026 releases consist mostly of dependency, CI (move to GitHub Actions) and security fixes; the documentation's release-notes page stops at v2.1.0 (2025-01-03) and upstream CI tests bitcoind 27.2.0 (v2.1.8 notes).

Bundled as a Python library (hwi==3.1.0 pinned in requirements since v2.1.10); BTCortex must not install HWI separately for Specter. Additions of HWI 3.2.0 (Jade Plus, BitBox02 Nova, testnet4) are therefore not part of Specter's USB path.

tor_type "custom" with proxy_url socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050 (and only_tor) routes outbound requests through BTCortex's Tor. tor_type "builtin" makes Specter install and run its own Tor daemon under <data folder>\tor-binaries, which BTCortex should avoid.

entries.security: Watch-only by default: keys stay on devices and PSBTs are signed on the device after explicit confirmation. However, Specter also offers a "Bitcoin Core (hot wallet)" device type that takes a mnemonic and imports xprv descriptors into a Core wallet under _hotstorage (protected only by an optional wallet passphrase); BTCortex must never create, pre-configure or recommend it. Authentication is off by default and the data folder (including node passwords and xpubs) is not encrypted at rest (warning added in 2.1.11). 2026 security fixes: open-redirect bypass (2.1.7), warning for known default secret keys (2.1.7), HWI bridge settings protected by auth and CSRF, API token validation and a ColdCard Mk3 seed-entropy advisory warning (2.1.11). Release verification: SHA256SUMS signed with the "Specter Signer 2026" OpenPGP key 9DC3 3CA8 3058 9DE3 B322 5C26 EEF5 756B 2EA4 2349 (signed by k9ert's key, published on keyserver.ubuntu.com). The Electron fallback download checks the extracted specterd against a pinned SHA-256 but not OpenPGP. The UTXO scan contacts an external block explorer (privacy).

entries.security: Verify the archive's OpenPGP signature against the Tor Browser Developers key (primary fingerprint EF6E 286D DA85 EA2A 4BA7 DE68 4E2C 6E87 9329 8290; 15.0.25 was signed with subkey 022D A248 432D 2A0E 0F54 E65E 316C 1FAC D62D 07D9) and the SHA-256 in the signed sha256sums-signed-build.txt; Authenticode cannot be used because tor.exe is unsigned. Releases are frequent and often security-relevant (0.4.9.14 fixed several high-severity bugs), so the update channel matters. The ControlPort is equivalent to full control of tor and its onion-service keys; use SAFECOOKIE, keep the DataDirectory and cookie readable only by the user (HiddenServiceDirGroupReadable has no effect on Windows) and never expose SocksPort or ControlPort beyond loopback (the manual warns that a non-local SocksPort leaks traffic and creates an open proxy). hs_ed25519_secret_key is the onion identity and must be protected and backed up like a credential. Log at notice level or below (the manual warns that more verbose logs may provide sensitive information). Tor does not start from paths containing non-ASCII characters (issue #10416 open; the proposed fix MR !357 was closed unmerged). A Tor-only node is exposed to Sybil and eclipse risks on a smaller address set.

entries.name: Tor Browser
entries.purpose: Hardened Firefox ESR-based browser bundled with its own tor process, for browsing the web and onion services anonymously. Useful to BTCortex users for opening onion block explorers and web interfaces, but it is not a general-purpose managed Tor daemon.

maintenance.evidence: Tor Browser 15.0.25 published 2026-10-12 (Firefox ESR security updates, tor 0.4.9.14, OpenSSL 3.5.9); 15.0 was released on 2025-10-28 on Firefox ESR 140; 16.0 is in alpha (16.0a14 directory dated 2026-10-16).

platforms.windowsDistribution: tor-browser-windows-x86_64-portable-15.0.25.exe and tor-browser-windows-i686-portable-15.0.25.exe (per-user portable installers) with detached .asc signatures by the Tor Browser Developers key; incremental and full .mar updates. Tor Browser 16.0 drops 32-bit x86.

entries.security: Downloads are signed with the same Tor Browser Developers key as the Expert Bundle. Tor Browser updates itself, changes its tor version without notice to other programs, and its tor exits when the browser closes, so services that depend on it break and onion services disappear. Routing other applications through Tor Browser's SOCKS port mixes their circuits with browsing. BTCortex must only launch it (for example to open an onion explorer URL) and must never read its cookie or control its tor.

entries.name: Trezor (Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3, Model T, Model One)
entries.purpose: Open-source hardware signing devices from SatoshiLabs. The device holds the seed, shows addresses and transaction details on its own screen and signs Bitcoin transactions only after on-device confirmation; host software (Trezor Suite, HWI, Sparrow, Electrum and others) talks to it over USB, and over Bluetooth on the Safe 7.

maintenance.evidence: core/CHANGELOG.md lists core firmware 2.12.5 dated 16 September 2026 (2.12.4 on 19 August, 2.12.3 on 24 July, 2.12.2 on 22 July, 2.12.1 on 17 June, 2.12.0 on 21 May 2026); data.trezor.io lists 2.12.5 for T3T1 (Safe 5, 19 entries) and T3W1 (Safe 7, 12 entries starting at 2.9.3, dated 21 October 2025 in the changelog). Legacy firmware for the Model One: 1.14.1 dated 18 March 2026. Repository trezor/trezor-firmware not archived, last push 2026-10-20. trezor.io/compare sells Safe 7, Safe 5 and Safe 3; the Model T and Model One are 'retired from sale, not from support' (critical security updates until at least 2036; Model T feature updates until at least 2031; Model One maintenance only).

latestStableRelease.version: core firmware 2.12.5 (Safe 3, Safe 5, Safe 7, Model T); legacy firmware 1.14.1 (Model One, 2026-03-18)

platforms.windowsDistribution: No vendor driver: both firmware lines expose Microsoft WinUSB compatible-ID descriptors (legacy/winusb.c, core/embed/io/usb/stm32/usb.c), so Windows binds WinUSB to the WebUSB interface automatically; very old Model One firmware/bootloaders use USB HID. Firmware installation, device setup, Bitcoin-only firmware and Safe 7 Bluetooth pairing are done in Trezor Suite (trezor-suite). The standalone Trezor Bridge is deprecated (trezor-bridge) and is not needed by HWI.

dependencies.notes: Required for firmware installation and updates, initial setup, switching to Bitcoin-only firmware, device authenticity checks and Safe 7 Bluetooth pairing.
Host software that exports xpubs/descriptors, displays addresses and sends PSBTs for on-device signing. HWI 3.2.0 does not support the Safe 7 (THP not implemented; HWI issue #775 open).
The deprecated standalone Bridge (127.0.0.1:21325) can hold the device; Trezor asks users to uninstall it.

entries.security: Open-source firmware and bootloader; firmware images are signed by SatoshiLabs and data.trezor.io publishes per-image fingerprints (for example 2.12.5 Safe 5 universal 7fff55b9…692d, Bitcoin-only e84f251b…b5c7) for reproducible-build checks. Secure elements: the Safe 3, Safe 5 and Safe 7 use an EAL6+ certified secure element (named as Optiga on the Safe 7 page); the Safe 7 adds the TROPIC01 chip (and post-quantum SLH-DSA-128 firmware/boot verification according to Trezor). The Model One and Model T have no secure element. Advisories: Ledger Donjon's Safe 3 evaluation (reported 2024-11-12) bypassed some supply-chain countermeasures by voltage glitching (Safe 5 not affected); Ledger Donjon's TROPIC01 laser fault-injection finding (Trezor response 2026-06-03) cannot be fixed in firmware but, according to Trezor, exposes no PIN, funds or backup. Firmware security fixes relevant to Bitcoin: 2.8.7 (2025-01-22) forbids multisig-to-singlesig change and per-node paths in multisig change/receive and removed 'Unchained Capital's multisig path'; 2.10.0 (2026-01-21) BIP-39 side-channel fix; 2.11.0 (2026-03-18) multisig verification bug fix; 2.12.2 (2026-07-22) external input misidentification and new external outputs in replacement transactions; legacy 1.14.0 BIP-39 side-channel fix and 1.14.1 advanced recovery for mnemonics shorter than 24 words. For BTCortex: never ask for the PIN, passphrase or recovery words; let passphrases be entered on the device; treat device_id and label as personal data (do not log); never flash firmware itself; every signing request must be started explicitly by the user and confirmed on the device.

entries.name: Wasabi Wallet
entries.purpose: Open-source, privacy-focused single-signature Bitcoin desktop wallet with a built-in WabiSabi CoinJoin client, bundled Tor and client-side BIP157/BIP158 compact-block-filter synchronisation. It can use the user's own Bitcoin Core node over JSON-RPC for filters, blocks, fee estimates and broadcasting.

maintenance.evidence: Wasabi Wallet v2.8.4 published 2026-10-13 (v2.8.3 2026-09-14, v2.8.0 2026-06-27, v2.7.0 2025-08-30). Latest master commit 2026-10-21 ('Remove Indexer (#15190)', author lontivero). Repository WalletWasabi/WalletWasabi is not archived. zkSNACKs Ltd., the original developer, discontinued its default CoinJoin coordinator on 2024-06-01 and the repository moved from zkSNACKs to the self-named WalletWasabi organisation with v2.0.8 (2024-06-01). Development has continued since: releases are published by the WalletWasabi organisation and the Windows MSI is Authenticode-signed by maintainer Lucas Ontivero.

platforms.windowsVersions: Windows 10 1607 or later and Windows 11 23H2 or later (2.8.4 release notes)
platforms.windowsDistribution: Wasabi-2.8.4.msi (99 340 288 bytes; WiX, InstallScope perMachine, Platform x64, default folder C:\Program Files\WasabiWallet\, Authenticode signer shown as Lucas Ontivero; MajorUpgrade blocks downgrades; UpgradeCode {D8E80773-D8CF-4031-B8B3-AA750AF0B413}) and Wasabi-2.8.4-win-x64.zip (96 203 518 bytes, self-contained, no installer). Every file has a detached .asc signature; SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.asc and SHA256SUMS.wasabisig cover the set. Executables: wassabee.exe (GUI) and wassabeed.exe (headless daemon). The website links only the MSI for Windows. No Windows arm64 build (arm64 exists for macOS and Linux only).

dependencies.notes: Own node over RPC: server=1, blockfilterindex=1 (compatible with pruning), RPC on loopback with cookie or rpcauth credentials. Without it Wasabi uses P2P compact filters from random peers.
Wasabi bundles and runs its own Tor by default. With UseTor=EnabledOnlyRunning it connects to an already-running Tor instead; avoid two Tor instances competing for the same SOCKS/control ports.
HWI ships inside Wasabi (2.0.8 updated it to 3.0.0, 2.3.0 to 3.1.0); BTCortex does not need to install it for Wasabi.
Hardware wallets via HWI over USB, or Coldcard via PSBT files on microSD. CoinJoin is not possible with hardware-wallet keys.

entries.security: Privacy relies on Tor plus client-side filtering; the documentation strongly advises against disabling Tor. CoinJoin needs a third-party coordinator that the user chooses: since 2.2.0 the client only joins rounds without a coordination fee and pays only mining fees, the coordinator sets the round's mining fee rate (capped by MaxCoinJoinMiningFeeRate, default 50) and may receive decomposition leftovers of up to 10 000 sats; WabiSabi prevents the coordinator from linking inputs to outputs, but it sees registered inputs and can ban them. BTCortex must never pick a coordinator. JSON-RPC has no TLS, some methods work without the wallet password because the wallet file is readable, and send/startcoinjoin carry passwords in request bodies: keep it disabled unless needed and never log its traffic. Release verification: per-file .asc and SHA256SUMS.asc signed with the zkSNACKs OpenPGP key 6FB3 872B 5D42 292F 5992 0797 8563 4832 8949 861E (RSA-2048, 'zkSNACKs <zksnacks@gmail.com>', valid until 2028-02-24; PGP.txt in the repository), still used for 2.8.x per the installation guide; the MSI is Authenticode-signed (Lucas Ontivero). 2.8.4 deprecates the 'compatibility passphrase' feature (users seeing its warning should create a new wallet) and ignores headers from longer chains with less accumulated work. Legal context (neutral): zkSNACKs blocked US persons from its websites and products in April 2024 and stopped coordinating on 2024-06-01 citing the need for more legal certainty; whether operating or using a CoinJoin coordinator is regulated depends on the jurisdiction (compare the 2025 US convictions of the Samourai Wallet founders for conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business).

entries.security: Installation, tunnel services and driver need administrator rights, so the zero-touch rule cannot be met without one UAC approval. Private keys live in .conf or DPAPI-protected .conf.dpapi files. The peer operator (or VPN provider) sees all traffic metadata and, for full-tunnel configurations, all destinations: never label a WireGuard connection as anonymous. PreUp/PostUp scripts run only when an administrator enables a registry key.
